title: RSA Encryption: Public and Private Keys, OAEP, and Three Myths
description: Encrypt with the recipient's public key and decrypt with the matching private key. Learn how padding and key size set byte limits, and troubleshoot tool errors.
content:
Encrypt with the recipient's public key and decrypt with the matching private key. The tool uses OAEP with SHA-256. Each 2048-bit key it generates can encrypt up to 190 bytes at a time. Use symmetric encryption for long messages and files, and use RSA only to wrap the symmetric key.

Generate and use a public and private key pair

To receive an encrypted message, generate a key pair and share your public key with the sender. The sender uses that key to turn plaintext into ciphertext. When you receive the ciphertext, use the matching private key to recover the plaintext. To send an encrypted message, get the recipient's public key. The person who needs to read the plaintext is the person who provides the public key. For messages in both directions, each person keeps their own private key and encrypts with the other person's public key.

Use temporary keys to try the workflow. Open the RSA encryption tool and select “Generate Key Pair (2048)”. The status reads “Key pair generated”, and the public and private keys appear in separate PEM fields. The tool generates public keys in SPKI format and private keys in PKCS#8 format. Use those same formats when importing existing test keys. [S2][S4]

Encrypt and decrypt a test message

Enter a short test message in “Plaintext / Ciphertext (Base64)”. Leave the public key in place and select “Encrypt”. When the status reads “Encryption complete”, copy the ciphertext from the “Result” panel. Replace the original input with the ciphertext, leave the matching private key in place, and select “Decrypt”. The original message should appear in the result field. Both operations share the input field, so verify its contents before selecting a button. If a colleague needs to reproduce the test, save a separate copy of the ciphertext used for decryption. Encrypting again overwrites the result, which makes the samples easy to mix up.

Base64 represents the ciphertext bytes as text so you can copy and share them. [S5] To see how the encoding works, try encoding and decoding a sample with the Base64 tool. Decoding the RSA output yields the ciphertext bytes. Recovering the original message requires decryption with the matching private key.

First misconception: Encrypting with a private key creates a signature

Encryption limits who can read a message. A signature lets a verifier confirm that the signature corresponds to the message and the public key. In encryption, the recipient uses their private key to decrypt. In signing, the sender uses their own private key to sign. The verifier uses the sender's public key, the message, and the signature. The private key holder has a different role in each operation. [S1][S3]

Node documents privateEncrypt, but do not assemble a signing flow from the function name. Node also provides sign and verify, and the specification defines separate signature schemes such as RSA-PSS. To verify a signature, confirm the agreed scheme and inputs. The tool's “Decrypt” button performs decryption only. [S1][S3]

Second misconception: Key size in bits gives plaintext capacity in bytes

Convert the modulus size from bits to bytes, then subtract the OAEP encoding overhead. The maximum is k − 2 × hLen − 2 bytes, where k is the RSA modulus size in bytes and hLen is the hash output size in bytes. A 2048-bit modulus is 2048 ÷ 8 = 256 bytes, and SHA-256 produces 32 bytes. The resulting limit is 256 − 2 × 32 − 2 = 190 bytes. [S1][S3]

In the Node boundary test, 190 bytes encrypted and decrypted back to the original input. Encryption failed at 191 bytes. The tool encodes input as UTF-8, so count the bytes after encoding. For the same sample, use new TextEncoder().encode(text).length. Each English letter in the test takes one byte, and “汉” takes three bytes. Adding Chinese characters can exceed the byte limit even if the character count matches an English-only sample. For multiline input, count the entire string. The tool preserves spaces and line breaks in plaintext, and counting only visible characters can miss them. [S2][S3]

Third misconception: RSA padding schemes are interchangeable

RSAES-PKCS1-v1_5 and RSAES-OAEP are encryption schemes with different encoding rules. You can use the same public key to compare them. Decrypting ciphertext with OAEP fails if it was produced with the other scheme. OAEP also requires a hash choice. In the Node test, the same 2048-bit public key encrypted 245 bytes with PKCS#1 v1.5 and failed at 246 bytes. Each scheme has its own limit. Document the padding scheme and OAEP hash in the interface agreement. [S1][S2][S3]

Use OAEP for new interfaces. The browser's Web Crypto encryption API supports OAEP, so the browser and receiver can agree on OAEP parameters. When setting up a new interface, send a test message using the tool's fixed OAEP and SHA-256 settings, then decrypt it on the receiving end with the same parameters. If a legacy interface explicitly requires PKCS#1 v1.5 encryption, verify compatibility in an environment that supports it. The specification also names a PKCS#1 v1.5 signature scheme, so confirm with the interface owner which encryption scheme the interface requires. [S1][S2]

What padding and key size control

This page has no padding-scheme or key-size dropdowns. “Generate Key Pair (2048)” sets the modulus size for new keys. Imported keys retain their own modulus size. The tool specifies RSA-OAEP with SHA-256 when importing either key, so importing a different key leaves the padding and hash settings in place.

In a configurable interface, select the padding scheme agreed with the recipient, then use the actual modulus size and hash to calculate capacity. Both padding and hash must match the settings used to produce the ciphertext. If the receiver uses a different key pair, changing parameters cannot make the keys match. When troubleshooting, record which public key produced the ciphertext so you can verify the pair directly. [S1][S2]

Troubleshoot input, size, and key mismatches

Start with the status message. Before encrypting, the tool verifies that the public key and plaintext are present. Before decrypting, it verifies that the private key and ciphertext are present. When encryption throws an exception, the tool prefixes the browser's message with “Encryption failed:”. Node uses a different API. In this test, oversized input produced error:0200006E:rsa routines::data too large for key size. Look for that exact text in Node logs. To distinguish a size issue from a format issue, keep the original public key and try shorter plaintext. If the shorter sample succeeds, measure the original input in bytes. [S2][S3]

Tool messageWhat to verify first
Please fill in the public key and plaintextVerify that the public key field is filled in and that the input field contains the text to encrypt.
Please fill in the private key and ciphertextVerify that the private key field is filled in and that the input field contains the ciphertext from the result field.
Encryption failed:Retry with a shorter sample. If it still fails, verify the public key format and record the browser message that follows.
Decryption failed: key mismatch or corrupted ciphertextVerify that the private key matches the public key used for encryption, that the ciphertext is intact, and that the sender used the agreed padding and hash.

The tool uses the same error message for key import and decryption failures. First verify that a short sample works with a single temporary key pair, then retry with the test input you need to troubleshoot. After a failure, the result field may still contain the previous output. Verify that the current operation succeeded before copying the result.

Use hybrid encryption for long messages and files

As the payload grows, handle the data and the key separately. Encrypt the data with a symmetric key. For example, verify the process with a sample in an environment that supports AES-GCM. Wrap the symmetric key with the recipient's RSA public key, then send the wrapped key and the encrypted data. The recipient uses their private key to recover the symmetric key and uses that key to decrypt the data. [S2][S6]

The size of the RSA input then depends on the key being wrapped. You can use the same workflow for a short message and for longer messages later. When testing an interface, verify each operation separately. First recover the test symmetric key, then verify that it decrypts the data. You can also practice symmetric encryption and decryption separately in the symmetric encryption tool. Record the symmetric algorithm separately from the RSA parameters in your test notes. Use the agreed hybrid encryption format to carry both parts and keep the payload out of RSA's input. [S1][S6]

Scope and limitations

This guide makes no security guarantees. RSA provides no forward secrecy when you use a long-term RSA key for encryption or key wrapping. Someone who saves old ciphertext and later obtains the matching private key can decrypt that ciphertext or recover the symmetric key used for the old message. Changing the sample text between operations leaves this limitation in place. [S3][S6]

Keep production private keys out of web tools. For browser demonstrations, generate temporary keys on the spot and use test data. To troubleshoot production compatibility, prepare a test key pair with the same formats and parameters, then verify encryption and decryption with a sample. Use only test material in screenshots, tickets, and logs. The temporary keys appear in the text fields after generation. Before sharing your screen or copying a screenshot, verify that the displayed key pair was generated for the demonstration and can be discarded afterward.

Before you retest

Start by isolating the failed operation. For encryption failures, verify the public key format, then the input byte count. For decryption failures, start with a short sample that decrypts successfully and change one input at a time to isolate key, ciphertext, and padding differences.

When handing a sample to a colleague, include the details below. Recovering the original plaintext in their environment confirms that the test data and parameters work for the full round trip. Use the same sample as a starting point when moving to another interface. Include the retest result and any new error message so your colleague can reproduce the operation under the same conditions.

  • Who holds the private key and which matching public key the sender used.
  • The agreed padding and hash, and the input size in bytes after encoding.
  • Whether the data sent is the Base64 representation of the raw ciphertext or another agreed format.
  • The status message and whether the failure occurred during encryption or decryption.

faqs.q: Who uses the public key and who uses the private key?
faqs.a: The sender encrypts with the recipient's public key. The recipient keeps the matching private key and uses it to decrypt.

faqs.q: Why can't the generated key encrypt long messages?
faqs.a: With OAEP-SHA256, a 2048-bit key generated by the tool can encrypt up to 190 bytes at a time, measured after UTF-8 encoding.
